newsitem.title: USA: Clinton nominates two economists to Fed board.
newsitem.headline: Clinton nominates two economists to Fed board.

text.p: President Clinton said on Thursday he would nominate University of Michigan professor Edward Gramlich and economic consultant Roger Ferguson to the board of the powerful Federal Reserve.
The long-awaited nominations, which are subject to Senate confirmation, are not expected to have much impact on the central bank's interest rate policy in the short run.
If approved by lawmakers, Ferguson will be only the third black to serve on the Fed's seven-person board and the first since Emmett Rice left the central bank at the end of 1986.

The two men will be filling posts that have been vacant since early this year when Janet Yellen departed to become White House chief economist and Lawrence Lindsey joined a conservative think tank here.

Neither Ferguson nor Gramlich are known to have strong views on monetary policy and thus are likely to defer -- at least initially -- to influential Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan when it comes to setting interest rates, analysts said.
Administration officials had first disclosed Clinton's plans to nominate the two economists back in April. They have been undergoing extensive security checks since then.
Gene Sperling, who heads Clinton's National Economic Council, described the nominees as "sound and pragmatic" and voiced hopes they would win Senate confirmation.
"All the feedback I've gotten was positive," he told reporters.

Democratic Sen. Tom Harkin, a long-time Fed critic, said he would review the nominations closely. "Americans need a more growth-oriented Federal Reserve," the Iowa lawmaker said. "For too long, this Greenspan Fed has restrained growth."

Ferguson, 45, has both a law degree and a Ph.D. in economics from Harvard University. A native of Washington D.C., Ferguson has been a partner since 1991 at New York-based international consultants McKinsey and Co. Inc., where he has specialized in financial issues.

Among his projects there: designing a super-regional bank strategy for a major commercial bank; helping a California savings bank consolidate operations after an acquisition; and working with a brokerage house on information technology.
Sperling said Ferguson was particularly impressive during his interview and commended his up-to-date knowledge of information technology, including currency payment systems.

Gramlich, 58, is a seasoned economist known for his pragmatism and consensus building. No stranger to Washington, he was a Fed researcher in the 1960s and served a brief stint here as deputy and acting director of the Congressional Budget Office in 1986 and 1987.

For the past two years, the economist has been best known as chairman of the federal government's Advisory Council on Social Security, which in January issued a report on ways to plug the pension system's future financing gap.
"Gramlich is one of the big-name economists in the country who has had serious public policy experience," Sperling said.

Gramlich has been nominated to fill the post vacated by Yellen and to represent the Richmond Fed district on the central bank's board. If confirmed by the Senate, his tenure would extend until Jan. 31, 2008.
Ferguson would represent the Boston region and would fill Lindsey's slot, which expires on Jan. 31, 2000.
The Clinton administration will get a chance to nominate another person to the Fed board next year, when Susan Phillips' term expires on Jan. 31.
